column1: What is backpropagation, in one sentence?
column2: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation for a scalar loss defined by a composition of functions, implemented by composing adjoint linearizations in reverse topological order.

column1: In a neural net, what is backprop used to compute?
column2: Gradients of the loss with respect to parameters (and intermediate activations).

column1: What structure does backprop operate on?
column2: A computational graph (a directed acyclic graph).

column1: During the forward pass, what does backprop typically cache?
column2: Intermediate activations (values needed to compute local derivatives later).

column1: Why cache activations during the forward pass?
column2: So local Jacobians/derivatives can be computed efficiently during the backward pass.

column1: What ordering does backprop use in the backward pass?
column2: Reverse topological order.

column1: What rule is repeatedly applied during backprop’s backward pass?
column2: The chain rule.

column1: In reverse-mode, what “thing” is propagated backward?
column2: Adjoints (sensitivities / cotangent vectors) of the loss w.r.t. node values.

column1: At each node, how is the incoming adjoint transformed?
column2: Multiply the upstream gradient by the local Jacobian (via a VJP, typically without building the full Jacobian).

Why is reverse-mode efficient for neural nets with many parameters?
column2: Because one backward pass gives gradients for all parameters when the output is a single scalar loss.

column1: Compared to reverse-mode, what’s the core inefficiency of forward-mode for many parameters?
column2: Forward-mode would require (roughly) a separate pass per parameter/direction to get all parameter gradients.

column1: What does VJP stand for?
column2: Vector-Jacobian Product.

column1: Conceptually, what does a VJP compute?
column2: Jᵀ v (Jacobian-transpose times a vector), without explicitly forming J.

column1: Why does VJP help avoid expensive Jacobian construction?
column2: It computes the needed product directly, often exploiting sparsity/structure, instead of materializing a (huge) Jacobian.

column1: For an element-wise operation, what special structure does the Jacobian have?
column2: It’s diagonal.

column1: For an element-wise operation, what does the VJP reduce to?
column2: A Hadamard (element-wise) product.

column1: For matrix multiplication / linear layers, why can we avoid explicit Jacobians?
column2: Closed-form gradient expressions exist (e.g., outer products / matmul identities).

column1: In your notes, what does “forward mode uses J_f x” mean?
column2: It pushes a tangent vector x forward through the Jacobian J_f (a JVP).

column1: In your notes, what does “reverse mode uses x = J_f^T y” mean?
column2: It pulls a cotangent vector y backward via J_fᵀ (a VJP).

column1: What’s the intuitive meaning of an adjoint in backprop (practical view)?
column2: Often “the transpose” action you apply when moving gradients backward through a linear map.

column1: For a linear map A: V → W, what direction does A push things?
column2: It pushes vectors forward: V → W.

column1: For a linear map A: V → W, what direction does the adjoint act?
column2: It pulls covectors/gradients backward: W* → V*.

column1: What is a “cotangent vector” in this context (plain language)?
column2: A gradient/sensitivity object that maps small changes in inputs to changes in scalar loss.

column1: Each node x →f y induces what two maps (geometric view)?
column2: A forward map on tangents and a backward map (pullback) on cotangents.

column1: In the notes, what is the backward (pullback) map’s type signature?
In the notes, what is the forward map’s type signature?
column2: f*: T_x → T_y.

column1: Fill in the pattern: backprop computes ∂L/∂x = ______ (∂L/∂y).
column2: f* (the pullback of f applied to the upstream gradient).

column1: When the network output is scalar loss L, what shape is the “Jacobian” of L w.r.t. a vector?
column2: It behaves like a row vector; the gradient is its transpose (a column vector).

column1: In your VJP section, what is J_W?
column2: The local Jacobian ∂y/∂W for a layer output y with respect to weights W.

column1: In your VJP section, what is ∇_y L?
column2: The upstream gradient: sensitivity of loss to the layer output y.

column1: State the general VJP form for weight gradients from your notes.
column2: ∇_W L = J_Wᵀ · (∇_y L).

column1: For a linear layer y = W x, what is the efficient expression for ∇_W L?
column2: ∇_W L = (∇_y L) xᵀ (an outer product).

column1: In one phrase: what does backprop “compose” during the backward pass?
column2: Adjoint linearizations (pullbacks) of each function, in reverse order.

column1: What’s the key difference between “error” (δ) in Nielsen’s framing and “adjoint” here?
column2: They refer to the same propagated sensitivity; δ is the historical/intuitional name for the adjoint.

column1: If you had to explain “upstream gradient” in one line, what is it?
column2: The gradient of the loss with respect to a node’s output, arriving from later computations.

column1: What does “reverse topological order” ensure during backprop?
column2: That when you process a node, all contributions from downstream nodes have already been accounted for.

column1: Why do “focused” prompts matter for SRS review?
column2: Overly broad prompts encourage partial recall and inconsistent answers; tight scope improves reliable retrieval.

column1: Why do “context-independent” prompts matter?
column2: Because cards are reviewed interleaved; the prompt must include enough context to be unambiguous on its own.
